steps.step: Analyse the problem and recall relevant learning outcomes
steps.script:
[S1] Welcome aboard! On this opening slide you can see the problem statement sitting proudly in the middle—"integral of x times sine of two x, from zero to pi divided by eight".
[S2] Oh wow, a definite integral with both algebra and trig bundled together.
[S1] Exactly. Before we swing our chalk, let’s unpack what you’ll need in your toolbox—kind of like checking you have a map, a torch, and snacks before entering a cave. 
[S2] Snacks? I’m in! What’s first on the checklist?
[S1] One—"integration by parts". Any time a lonely x is multiplied by a spicy trig function, that technique is our Swiss-army knife.
[S2] Got it. u v minus the integral of v d u, right?
[S1] Perfect recall. Two—basic trig integrals. We need to remember that the antiderivative of sine of two x is negative cosine of two x divided by two.
[S2] I can still hear my high-school teacher chanting that in my sleep.
[S1] Three—evaluating definite integrals. Once we have the antiderivative, we’ll plug in the upper limit pi divided by eight and the lower limit zero.
[S2] So the entire game plan is: choose u and d v cleverly, find v, rewrite, integrate again if needed, then slam in the limits.
[S1] That’s the roadmap. Quick warm-up question: looking at the first bullet under the problem, which factor would you nominate as u so that its derivative simplifies nicely?
[S2] I’d let u equal x because its derivative is just one—super simple.
[S1] Exactly—like choosing the lightest backpack for the hike. Great job! Anything feel mysterious so far?
[S2] Nope, just eager to try the parts formula.
[S1] Wonderful. Let’s stride to the next slide and set up the integration by parts.

steps.step: Choose the technique and set up integration by parts
steps.script:
[S1] On this slide the left column shows our choices: u equals x, d v equals sine of two x d x.
[S2] Which means d u is simply d x, and v is… let me integrate sine of two x…
[S1] Go for it—remember the chain rule when integrating.
[S2] The antiderivative should be negative cosine of two x divided by two.
[S1] Spot on. Many students forget that divide-by-two factor—cheeky little gremlin!
[S2] So plugging into u v minus integral v d u, I get x times negative cosine two x divided by two, minus the integral of negative cosine two x divided by two times d x.
[S1] Nicely stated. Notice how two negatives will eventually turn that second term positive.
[S2] Aha—minus a minus is plus. Algebraic sunshine!
[S1] Indeed. Pause and glance at the green highlight on the slide—see that fraction one over two? That’s the crucial constant travelling with us.
[S2] Right. Forgetting it would be like leaving the torch batteries at home.
[S1] Exactly, and we’d stumble in the dark. Anything you’d adjust before we continue?
[S2] I think we’re set. The first term is clear, the remaining integral is one half times the integral of cosine of two x.
[S1] Excellent. Let’s move on to simplifying that remaining integral.

[S1] Here the algebra unfolds. Focus on the line where the minus sign vanished.
[S2] Yup, we now have negative x times cosine of two x divided by two, evaluated from zero to pi over eight, plus one half integral of cosine two x d x.
[S1] Good. Want to handle that cosine integral?
[S2] Sure. The antiderivative of cosine two x is sine two x divided by two.
[S1] Perfect. Don’t lose the one half in front.
[S2] So the whole piece becomes one half times sine two x divided by two—that is sine two x over four.
[S1] Exactly—like stacking two filters: first one half, then another one half.
[S2] So we’ve traded a tougher integral for simpler functions we can plug limits into.
[S1] That’s the magic of integration by parts—turns a boulder into two small pebbles.
[S2] Pebbles ready! I’m itching to evaluate at the bounds.
[S1] Fantastic enthusiasm. Slide four, here we come.

steps.step: Evaluate the antiderivative at the bounds
steps.script:
[S1] The blackboard now shows F of x equals negative x cosine two x divided by two plus sine two x over four.
[S2] Upper limit first: x equals pi over eight. I’ll compute cosine of two x—that’s cosine of pi over four.
[S1] Which equals root two divided by two. Nicely spotted on the right-hand margin.
[S2] And sine of pi over four is also root two over two.
[S1] Symmetry can be beautiful, can’t it?
[S2] Plugging in, I get negative pi over eight times root two over two, all over two… Wait, let me write it neatly: negative pi times root two over thirty-two.
[S1] Good catch combining the denominators. And the second term becomes root two over two divided by four, which is root two over eight.
[S2] So F of pi over eight equals root two times four minus pi, all over thirty-two.
[S1] Very tidy! Now evaluate at the lower limit zero.
[S2] Easy—both pieces vanish, so F of zero is zero.
[S1] Therefore the definite integral is F of pi over eight minus zero, giving exactly what you just wrote.
[S2] That would be positive, right? Because four is bigger than pi.
[S1] Yes, about zero point eight six units bigger. Great internal check.
[S2] Awesome—answer in hand! What’s next—sanity check?
[S1] You read my mind. Final slide incoming.

steps.step: Check result and relate back to learning outcomes
steps.script:
[S1] Last slide: we list two quick validations. First, sign analysis—x is non-negative, sine of two x is non-negative on the interval, so area should be positive.
[S2] And our result root two times four minus pi over thirty-two is positive. Check!
[S1] Second, curriculum reflection. We successfully used "integration by parts" from the Integration—Continued unit.
[S2] Plus some chain-rule trig differentiation from the Functions and Differentiation unit.
[S1] Exactly. Quick numerical approximation—pop that into your calculator.
[S2] Crunching… I get about zero point zero three eight.
[S1] Reasonable magnitude for a small slice under the curve—great sanity tick.
[S2] Feels satisfying, like closing a well-written detective novel.
[S1] Beautiful analogy, Sherlock. Any lingering mysteries?
[S2] None—just proud of taming the integral dragon.
[S1] And you did it with flair! Keep that confidence for future adventures.
[S2] Thanks, mentor. Ready to tackle the next quest!
[S1] Fantastic. Until then, great job and take care.
